{{Short description|American mathematician}}
'''George James Minty Jr.''' (September 16, 1929, [[Detroit]] – August 6, 1986,<ref name=IUreport>{{cite web|url=http://webapp1.dlib.indiana.edu/iubot/view?docId=1986-09-06&chunk.id=d1e1634&toc.depth=1&toc.id=d1e785&brand=iubot|website=Minutes of the Board of Trustees of Indiana University|date=6 September 1986|title=Report of Death, George J. Minty Jr.}}</ref> [[Bloomington, Indiana]]) was an American mathematician, specializing in mathematical analysis and discrete mathematics. He is known for the [[Klee–Minty cube]], the [[Browder–Minty theorem]], the introduction of [[Oriented matroid|oriented regular matroids]], and the [[Minty-Vitaver theorem]] on [[graph coloring]].

==Biography==
[[File:Minty.png|thumb|400px|The beginning of Minty's article ''Monotone (nonlinear) operators in Hilbert space'', published in ''[[Duke Mathematical Journal]]'', 1962]]
George Minty Jr. grew up in Detroit. His father emigrated, after WW I, from Scotland to work in Detroit's automotive industry as a [[tool and die maker]]. George Minty Jr. received his bachelor's degree from Detroit's [[Wayne State University]].  After service in the [[Signal Corps (United States Army)|US Army Signal Corps]] at [[Fort Monmouth]],<ref name=Halmos>{{cite web|title=Who's That mathematician? Paul R. Halmos Collection - Page 35|website=Mathematical Association of America|url=https://www.maa.org/press/periodicals/convergence/whos-that-mathematician-paul-r-halmos-collection-page-35}}</ref> he became in 1956 a graduate student in mathematics at the [[University of Michigan]].<ref name=UMich>{{cite web|title=George J. Minty|website=Faculty History Project, University of Michigan|url=http://faculty-history.dc.umich.edu/faculty/george-j-minty}}</ref> There he received in 1959 his PhD with thesis ''Integrability Conditions for Vector Fields in Banach Spaces'' supervised by [[Erich Rothe]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy|name=George James Minty, Jr.|id=5068}}</ref> As a postdoc in 1959 he was briefly a visiting researcher at Tokyo's [[Waseda University]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Appreciation to Referees|journal=Operations Research|volume=7|issue=3|year=1959|pages=415–419|issn=0030-364X|doi=10.1287/opre.7.3.415|doi-access=free}}</ref>

{{blockquote|His first job out of grad school was as an applied mathematician at the General Motors Research Laboratory in Detroit, Michigan, and it was here that he first melded the discrete and the continuous to obtain significant results.<ref name=Halmos/>}}

Minty joined the University of Michigan faculty and was eventually promoted to associate professor before he resigned in 1965.<ref name=UMich/> For the academic year 1964–1965 he was on leave to do research at the [[Courant Institute]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Leaves of Absence|newspaper=The Michigan Daily|date=June 23, 1964|volume=74|issue=1|page=10|url=https://digital.bentley.umich.edu/midaily/mdp.39015071754092/14}}</ref> In 1965 he was awarded a [[Sloan Research Fellowship]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Past Fellows, Sloan Research Fellows|website=Alfred P. Sloan Foundation|url=https://sloan.org/past-Fellows?page=537}}</ref> At Indiana University he was a full professor of mathematics from 1965<ref>{{cite web|url=http://webapp1.dlib.indiana.edu/iubot/view?docId=1965-05-21&doc.view=print&toc.depth=1&toc.id=0&brand=iubot|title=Appointments to the Faculties|website=Minutes of the Board of Trustees of Indiana University|date=21 May 1965}}</ref> until his death in 1986.<ref name=IUreport/>

==Research==
Minty's 1966 paper ''On the axiomatic foundations of the theories of directed linear graphs, electrical networks and network-programming'' is important in [[matroid theory]]. In that 1966 paper, according to [[Dominic Welsh]]:

{{blockquote|The circuit space and cocircuit space of binary matroids were introduced by Minty ... who was also the first to study orientable matriods.<ref name="Welsh2010">{{cite book|author=Welsh, D. J. A.|title=Matroid Theory|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=QL2iYMBLpFwC&pg=PA181|page=181|date=1 January 2010|publisher=Courier Corporation|isbn=978-0-486-47439-7}}</ref>}}

According to K.-C. Chang:
{{blockquote|The theory of [[Monotone function#Monotonicity in functional analysis|monotone operator]]s and [[pseudo-monotone operator]]s attracted much attention in the 1960s and 70s. The works of Minty ..., Browder ..., [[Philip Hartman|Hartman]] and [[Guido Stampacchia|Stampacchia]] ..., [[Haïm Brezis|H. Brezis]] ..., etc. constitute the basic content of the theory.<ref name="Chang2006">{{cite book|author=Kung-Ching Chang|title=Methods in Nonlinear Analysis|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tUaWkBG0AD0C&pg=PA421|date=30 March 2006|publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-3-540-29232-6|page=421}}</ref>}}

In 2012 D. Erdős, A. Frank, and K. Kun published a sharpening of Minty's coloring theorem (published in 1962 in ''[[The American Mathematical Monthly]]'').<ref>{{cite arXiv|author=Erdős, Dóra|author2=Frank, András|author3=Kun, Krisztián|title=Sink-Stable Sets of Digraphs|year=2012|class=math.CO|eprint=1205.6071}} See page 6 for a statement (Theorem 3.2) of Minty's coloring theorem.</ref>
